newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Sandinistas up ante in three-day Nicaragua strike.
newsitem.headline: Sandinistas up ante in three-day Nicaragua strike.

text.p: Pro-Sandinista protesters raised the level of a three-day-old national strike against Nicaragua's right-wing government on Wednesday, burning tires, raising more barricades and shutting down some highways.

While the strike's affect on the capital was minimal, protesters blocked highways outside Managua, especially the southern stretch of the Panamerican highway, creating long lines of cargo-laden trucks, state radio reported.
Business leaders said the strike's effect on business so far had been minimal, but could increase if the strike lasted much longer.

"Their strategy is to strangle Managua, but the trucks have been getting through the barricades. So far it has not had a large impact on sellers," said Nicolas Garcia Baltodano, general manager of the Mercado Mayoreo, Nicaragua's largest grains, fruits and vegetables market.
Garcia told Reuters 90 percent of the supply trucks were arriving at the market, but if the road blockages lasted nine to 10 days more, there could be shortages.
Police said about 5,000 protesters had set up at least 25 barricades across Nicaragua, and late on Tuesday hooded gunmen burned a bus that was operating in spite of the strike call.

Strikers are protesting against the government's economic policies, which they say are pushing people out of work. They also want legal titles to confiscated property received during the Sandinista land reform.
"We take down the barricades and when we leave they put them back up again," police spokesman Capt. Justo Zamora told Reuters.

Late on Tuesday, President Arnoldo Aleman said if the strike ended he would cede to a Sandinista demand and present two proposed laws -- one to help resolve the property dispute, the other to prevent bank foreclosures on indebted farmers -- for debate by the National Assembly's legal commissions.
But Sandinistas remained sceptical and did not offer to end the strike after Aleman's concession.
"The reality is that Aleman conceded because he knew he didn't have sufficient votes in the National Assembly to approve these laws," Sandinista spokesman Silvio Mora said.

The return of burning tires and barricades has revived memories of the early days of Aleman's predecesser, former President Violeta Chamorro, when boisterous Sandinista street protests forced Chamorro to grant major concessions to the Sandinistas, who governed Nicaragua from 1979 to 1990.
